en: On the left-hand side,
At the edge of the endless desert,
Among the rough, broken ridges,
Upon a gaping promontory,
There is the famed land of Yarkand.
Dwelling in that Yarkand
Is the campaigning champion.
Tell Khan Zhortuulchu to gather his people
And come;
Let him not leave his old men behind,
And let him bring his children riding
As usual upon their packsaddles.
Skirting the hot desert,
Let him come properly to my feast,
Having shod his tulpars.
Tell him to come to my feast
And see this spectacle.
If he does not come to my feast,
If he does not see this spectacle,
I will raid and destroy his people;
I will leave his donkey braying in the ravine.
If he fails to come in his turn,
This is how I will settle his account.
Tell every people you see without fail.
When you travel farther,
Covering ground without sparing your horse,
In the city of Wide Urgench,
In the villages of broad Afghanistan,
Tell their Khan Akun,
And tell all the peoples you see there.
Say that Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Has camped at Üch-Karkyra;
Say that Kökötöy's great wealth
Has filled the face of the earth;
Say that Kökötöy's great feast
Has reached the time to be given!
Give Khan Akun my greetings;
Tell him to come to my feast.
If he does not come to my feast,
The clamorous shooting,
The struggle that cannot be healed—
Tell him to behold them from atop his house.
Tell him to surrender his beautiful daughter
As booty, without begrudging her!
Go no farther; turn back this way,
And return directly from that place.
With red banners and blue spears,
Let not one Kyrgyz remain behind.
When you head straight on from there,
You come to a place called Chambyl-Bel.
Dwelling in Chambyl-Bel
Are Zhanaaly and the hero Karach,
Who summer in Belendi
And tether their tulpars
Upon the ridge of Belendi.
They never shrink from death
Nor turn and flee from doom.
Say it is Khan Kökötöy's memorial feast,
The foremost of great gatherings;
Say the elder like a prophet,
The blessing-giving Khan Koshoy, the holy man,
Is the head of that feast.
Tell the iron-cored hero,
The swaying brave,
To come to my feast
And see this spectacle.
When the people move uphill,
When the horses' tongues turn black,
I will trample their heads
And scatter all four kinds of livestock.
I will destroy their lives
And send their children into uproar.
If they do not love this spectacle,
Tell them to come to my feast!
In that distant land,
In the midst of the Kara-Kum,
Is the sultan of spearmen,
Urum Khan's Kökbörü,
Who has taken spoils from many peoples,
A champion born surpassing
All his father's other sons.
Say Kökötöy's camp has settled
Along Üch-Karkyra.
Say the time has come for Chinese, Kalmyks, and Muslims
To grapple with one another;
There are champions and mounted combats,
A mighty bald champion comes from the Kalmyks,
A mighty bald champion comes from the Kyrgyz,
And these too compete for prizes,
Striking one another in the chest.
A naked woman untethers a camel;
If he does not see this spectacle,
The people will depart with their eyes opened.
Tell Urum Khan's Kökbörü
To come to my feast.
If he does not come to my feast,
I shall show him Kökötöy's red banner with its gray crescent
From atop his house,
And tumult crying from side to side.
If that arrogant man does not come,
If he delays, I will challenge him;
If he is very late,
I will whip him and start a quarrel!
When you turn back this way,
To the great holy city of sheikhs,
To mighty Kokand and Margalan,
To Kozubek of the Khan of Kokand,
Malabek of Margalan,
Fork-bearded Synzhybek of Andijan,
Alabek of Alty-Shaar,
And Sanchybek in Samarkand—
Give all of them my greetings.
Tell them to come, not one left behind!
If they should fail to hear,
Or hear yet pay no heed,
And lie idle unexpectedly,
If they do not see this spectacle,
If they do not come to my feast,
Tell them to die, not remain alive!
Tell them to behold Kökötöy's red banner with its golden crescent
From atop their own houses!
Tell them to give us
All their dark-eyed daughters as booty.
When you travel farther,
There is the renowned city of Bukhara.
Ruling that Bukhara
Is a khan named Temir Khan;
They have round baked bread
And houses with four corners.
Wearing his blue skullcap high,
Give Temir Khan my greetings.
Say it is Kökötöy's memorial feast,
The foremost of great gatherings.
Say the father of the people, hero Koshoy,
Is the chief directing the feast.
To see this spectacle,
Let none of their elders remain at home;
Let them all come out upon the road.
If they pay no ear to the words,
If they do not heed my command,
Tell them they will see a fine quarrel;
Tell every one of them to die.
If my anger should rise,
This Bukhara standing here—
I will trample its head
And scatter all four kinds of livestock.
I will slaughter its master where he stands;
By force I will slaughter his mares.
When they draw near, I will
Beat out the brains of every one.
I will make Bukhara pay
For its deeds of long ago.
On the far side of Bukhara
There is a place called Zheti-Özön.
Dwelling in Zheti-Özön
Are the people called Zhediger.
Among those Zhediger
Is their khan called Bagysh.
Let him tether his tulpar;
Let not one warrior remain.
Leveling their spears,
Urging on their thoroughbreds,
To Kökötöy's memorial feast,
Tell blue-maned Bagysh to come.
If he does not come to my feast,
If he does not see this spectacle,
I will simply wake him from sleep
And raid away his horses!
Tell him to know of this feast,
To cross here with his host,
And submit to what I say!
When you turn back from there,
There are reeds in the black desert;
He plays with palace maidens,
A fiddler in a house with daughters,
A cupbearer in a house with kumys;
There is maiden-adorned Agysh.
His strength is immense,
A peerless man born a hero.
Beneath him his chestnut tulpar
Fits him like a sleeve;
He perches without a wrist-rest
The white-shouldered eagle of Orolmo,
Which watches wolves and foxes.
Hero Agysh, no taller than an elbow,
Is sinew from head to foot,
A renowned and formidable man;
When he faces the Kara Kalmyks,
He is a man whose back reaches them.
Made wanton by his wealth,
Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Has camped at Üch-Karkyra, tell him.
Say there is meat like Ala-Too,
Broth like Ala-Köl,
And the time has come to give the feast.
Say there are all kinds of people
And wonders without end.
Tell him to come to my feast
And see this spectacle.
If he does not see this spectacle,
He is a woman-hearted man;
If he fails to take heed,
If by chance he does not come,
Tell him to behold Kökötöy's red banner with its golden crescent
From atop his own house,
And give us all the palace maidens
As booty!
When you travel farther,
Beyond Great Bukhara,
In a plain with a great river,
Dwelling among rugged hills,
Whose tale is extraordinary,
Called a merciless hero,
Is Muzburchak of Khan Buudayyk.
He steeped his spear in blood;
The man who came to grapple with him
He pressed into the black earth.
Meeting him head-on,
No foe escaped and emerged.
He girded his waist tightly,
Born greater than his father;
When his anger rose,
He cast the enemy into turmoil.
His weapons formed an armful upon his body—
Muzburchak of Khan Buudayyk.
No man defeated him in wrestling;
No one came facing me,
And he yielded his companion to no one.
He sowed his rice as an autumn crop;
When he wrestled an enemy,
He swallowed and chewed his windpipe.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
That elephant-built brute,
Muzburchak of Khan Buudayyk—
Give Muzburchak my greetings.
Tell him to come
To Kökötöy's renowned great feast
And see where unbelievers and Muslims
Gather together.
Tell him to see the poles crack in their hands
And bend.
Tell him to see the heroes charge on horseback
And joust.
Tell him to come to my feast
And see this spectacle!
If he does not come to my feast,
If he does not see this spectacle,
I will find a splendid quarrel.
Until the bylkıldak stalk ripens,
Until the autumn gossamer flies,
I will fight hard for six months.
I will load gunpowder
Upon Kökötöy's red-tailed black camel.
If he does not heed my words,
I will shoot from atop his house
And make Muzburchak buckle.
